place.zh: 沉鼎观 · 大比 · 对秦雁
place.en: Chending Temple · The contest · Against Qin Yan

setup.zh: 第三轮，对面是外门排头的秦雁：真灵根，六层，一口下阶的法器剑，剑气出去三尺。她在外门熬了三年，两回差一场进前四，今年再进不去，家里就熬不住了：「我不让你。你也别让我。」
setup.en: Round three, and across from you is Qin Yan, first on the outer register: true root, layer six, a low-tier magic sword whose breath reaches three feet past the point. Three years in the outer court, twice one bout short of the last four; if she misses this year, her family can't hold out. "I won't give way to you. Don't you give way to me."

recap.zh: 第三轮你对秦雁：她的剑，她的冰锥，你土墙挡冰，火打脚。三十招上她把你逼到台边，袖子里的雷符始终没掏——剑尖往前一送，你拿左臂接了，一把攥住她的剑鞘，两个人一齐往外一歪，她先落了地。
recap.en: In round three you fought Qin Yan: against her sword and her ice spikes you raised earth to stop the ice and threw fire at her feet. At the thirtieth move she drove you to the edge, the thunder talisman in her sleeve never drawn — when the point came forward you took it through your left arm, seized her scabbard, and the two of you tipped out together; she landed first.

en: First on the outer register: Qin Yan, layer six.
"I won't give way to you. Don't you give way to me."

story.zh:
第三轮，马小宝对鲁泥鳅。鲁泥鳅上台前，从小满身边挤过去，压低了嗓子：「昨儿我下山去船上看我爹。那面镜子，是我爹的船从下邳捎上来的——马三老爷雇的是我爹的船——在我爹船舱里搁了一路。红布底下，半夜里自己亮过一回——冷的，像泗水底下的光。我爹说，那不是照妖的，是认东西的。」说完，他搓了搓手，上台去了。鲁泥鳅是渔户的儿子，水性好，身子滑，头一拳便钻到了马小宝腋下。马小宝这才摘下了铜镜。

小满站在台下，看得清清楚楚：那面镜子，不是一举就亮的。马小宝两手捧着它，脸上的斑「腾」地一红，一片一片鼓起来，像是有人往他身子里抽东西，抽出来，灌进镜子里——镜面这才亮了，一道黄光扑在鲁泥鳅脸上。鲁泥鳅「哎哟」一声，捂着眼睛倒退，嘴里直叫：「冷的！那光是冷的，往心口钻！」他退一步，马小宝又照一回，斑又红一回，喘得两个肩膀一耸一耸；照到第三回，鲁泥鳅一脚踩空，跌下了台。马小宝捧着镜子，站在那里喘了好一会儿，才喘匀。他冲台下的小满扬了扬下巴。

小满对的，是秦雁。

台角的水缸边上，两个人碰上了。秦雁舀了半瓢水，没喝，递给了他。小满接过来喝了，道：「秦师姐。秘境里那一回……」秦雁道：「你没往下坠。我记得。」她又舀了一瓢，自己喝了，望着台上那炷香，「你知道我为什么非进前四不可？」小满摇头。秦雁道：「进了内门，一月十块灵石，能折银子寄家。我爹前年叫熊把腿咬了，躺到如今。今年再进不去，家里就熬不住了。」她把瓢放回缸沿上，看着他，「我不让你。你也别让我。」

小满捧着那瓢，半天没说出话来。他把瓢放下。秦雁点了点头，先上了台。

小满跟着上了台。秦雁比他高半个头，两道眉毛长而直，像两口出了鞘的剑，从来没描过；脸是晒黑了的，猎户家的姑娘，一点脂粉也不搽。她平日不大笑，一张脸冷冷的。她一上台，台下内门那一片，先静了一半。小满先看的却是她的脚：站得真稳，脚底下像钉了钉子。秦雁道：「沈师弟，听说你只有四层。」小满道：「是。」秦雁道：「我说过，不让。」小满道：「我打不过，会跑的。」秦雁一愣，随即笑了，嘴角露出一颗虎牙，跟那张冷脸怎么也对不上，倒比不笑的时候好看。
story.en:
Third round: Ma Xiaobao against Lu the Loach. Before going up, Lu squeezed past Xiaoman and said low: "Yesterday I went down to see my father on his boat. That mirror came up from Xiapi on my father's boat — Master Ma San hired my father's boat — and it sat in his hold all the way. Under the red cloth, one night, it lit up by itself — cold, like the light at the bottom of the Si. My father says it isn't for showing demons, it's for recognising things." Then he rubbed his hands and went up. Lu was a fisherman's son, slippery as his name, and his first punch ducked in under Ma Xiaobao's arm. Only then did Ma Xiaobao take off the mirror.

Below the stage Xiaoman saw it clearly: the mirror didn't light just by being raised. Ma Xiaobao held it in both hands, and the blotches on his face flared red and swelled patch by patch, as if something were being drawn out of him and poured into the mirror — only then did its face light, and a beam of yellow light hit Lu in the face. Lu yelped and staggered back clutching his eyes: "Cold! That light's cold — it goes for your heart!" He backed a step; Ma Xiaobao lit it again, the blotches flared again, and his shoulders heaved; at the third flash Lu missed his footing and fell off the stage. Ma Xiaobao stood holding the mirror, panting a long while before he got his breath. He jerked his chin at Xiaoman below.

Xiaoman's bout was against Qin Yan.

By the water vat at the corner of the stage the two of them met. Qin Yan ladled half a scoop and didn't drink it; she handed it to him. Xiaoman drank. "Sister Qin. That time in the hidden realm…" "You didn't hang. I remember." She ladled another and drank it herself, watching the incense on the stage. "Do you know why I have to make the last four?" Xiaoman shook his head. "In the inner court it's ten stones a month, and you can change them into silver and send it home. Two years ago a bear took my father's leg; he's been lying down ever since. If I don't get in this year, my family can't hold out." She set the ladle on the vat's rim and looked at him. "I won't give way to you. Don't you give way to me."

Xiaoman held the ladle and couldn't say a word for a long time. He set the ladle down. Qin Yan nodded and went up onto the stage first.

Xiaoman followed her up. Qin Yan stood half a head taller than him, her two brows long and straight like two blades out of the scabbard, never pencilled; her face was sun-darkened — a hunter's daughter, no powder at all. She seldom smiled, and her face was cold. When she stepped up, half the inner-court men below went quiet. Xiaoman looked at her feet first: she stood very steady, as if nailed to the stone. "Brother Shen, I hear you're only at layer four." "Yes." "I told you: I won't give way." "If I can't win, I'll run." Qin Yan was startled, then laughed — one tiger tooth showed at the corner of her mouth, which didn't match that cold face at all, and made her better-looking than when she didn't smile.

label.en: Watch her feet; last thirty moves

exits.means: fights Qin Yan, outlasting her moves; at the edge takes her thrust through his left arm, seizes her scabbard, and she lands off the stage first

withdrawn.zh: 秦雁把剑收回半寸，退后一步：「再来。」
withdrawn.en: Qin Yan draws her sword back half an inch and steps back. "Again."

story.zh:
这一场，跟方才那一场大不一样。秦雁的剑是真剑，招是真招——那是一口下阶的法器，在她手里，剑尖递出去，剑上那一道青气还要往前再走三尺，人在一丈开外，剑气已到了跟前。一剑一剑递过来，又快又稳，逼得台下的人屏住了气。小满不看她的剑，看她的脚：剑往哪里去，脚先往哪里挪；脚往哪里挪，肩膀先往哪里沉。可她的脚，比卢方的干净得多，挪得又小又快，他看得见，身子总慢半步。第七招，剑尖挑破了他的袖子；第十五招，挑破了他的肩头；第二十招上，一道血口子从他右颊上拉过去，热乎乎的，淌进了领子里。他两只手里扣着诀，挡不得，只能躲，东一跳，西一滚，躲得极难看，有两回简直是连滚带爬。

第二十二招上，秦雁左手一捻，三根冰锥齐齐射了过来。小满一掌按在青石板上，身前拱起一片土墙，冰锥「噗噗噗」扎进土里；另一只手里已经冒出一团火，朝她脚底下打过去——她跳开的那一霎，他抢回了半步。台下有人叫起来：「两样！又是两样！」秦雁落了地，看了他一眼，那一眼里，是吃了一惊。

有一剑来得太快，他来不及看脚，只得往后一仰，剑尖贴着他的鼻子过去，削下了他额前的一绺头发。那绺头发在半空里飘啊飘，飘到台下，正落在阿禾的小本子上。阿禾低头看了一眼，把它夹进了本子里，面无表情。她拿笔的那只手，大拇指的指甲，一直掐在另一只手的掌心里。

可躲着躲着，小满觉出一样东西来，是他打记事起没有过的：他在笑。剑尖一回一回从他鼻子底下、耳朵边上过去，他浑身是口子，肋下那根骨头一喘一疼，嘴角却是往上的——这是头一回，对面站着一个比他强的人，一招一招都是真的，不藏，不让，不图他什么。他跟着那口剑转，像跟着爹在林子里追一头最好的鹿，追得心口发烫。台下的人起先屏着气，后来有人叫了一声好，再后来，一片一片地叫起来。

三十招上，他到底给逼到了台边。脚后跟底下，青石板只剩半寸，再往后，是冻土。秦雁的剑尖，抵在了他喉咙上，凉丝丝的。台下静了。

秦雁右手的袖子里，一直扣着一张黄纸雷符，符上的朱砂纹里有一线细细的蓝光游来游去，从第一招扣到这时候，始终没有掏出来。小满离她只有一剑远，看得见袖口里露出来的那一角。她往台下看了一眼：头一排蹲着几个刚进门的小孩子，正张着嘴看她，挤在台沿底下，离那几块青石板，不到一臂。那张符，她没有掏。小满的右手垂在袖子里，指头碰着了那三根痒痒针，碰了一碰，松开了。

她不用掏。剑尖抵在他喉咙上，她只要往前送一寸，他便只有往后退，一退，便下去了。阿禾那张纸上写的就是这一寸：两回大比，赢的四场，场场如此。这一寸要来，他早晨在灶口就知道了；拿什么去换，是他自己定的。

小满没有退。剑尖往前一送的那一霎，他往前迎了上去——不是迎喉咙，是把身子一侧，拿左臂去接。剑尖从他左臂外侧扎了进去，从另一边透了出来，疼得他眼前白了一片。可他人已经到了秦雁跟前，拿那只透着剑的左手，一把攥住了她左手里那截剑鞘。

秦雁一惊，抽剑，剑卡在他胳膊里，抽不动；她撒手弃剑，一掌劈向他手腕，他不放；两个人便在台边上扭成了一团，没有招，只有手、肘、肩膀、膝盖，像两个在泥地里抢一只兔子的孩子。她一肘撞在他胸口上，撞着一块硬东西，是烫的。秦雁比他高，比他稳，三下两下，已把他压得半个身子悬在台外。小满脚下一勾——猎户下套子勾兔子腿的那一下——勾住了她的脚踝。两个人一齐往外一歪。

小满左手攥着剑鞘，右手扒住了石沿。秦雁的脚尖，在台边上点了一点，没点住。

她落在了台下的冻土上，站着落的，一步也没踉跄。小满挂在石沿上，半个身子在外头，左臂上还插着她的剑。那炷香，只剩一点红了。

执事咽了一口唾沫，敲锣：「……秦雁出台。沈小满，胜。」

台下先是一静，跟着便是一片吼声，比方才扔卢方的那一声还响，一浪一浪，从演武场这一头滚到那一头。

秦雁站在台下，低头看了看自己的手，又抬起头来看小满，看了好一会儿。小满爬上来，拔出胳膊里那口剑，倒转了剑柄，连那截剑鞘一并递给她，压低了声音：「师姐。」秦雁接过剑，道：「掉下台的，输。规矩上，就是输了。」她看了一眼他垂着的手，低声道：「四层的人，躲不过我三十招。你那双眼睛，不是练出来的。」小满道：「师姐也是。」他看了一眼她的袖口。秦雁的眉毛轻轻一挑，拿左手把袖口按了一按，没接这话，又道：「你那几步，是猎户的步子吧？」小满一怔：「师姐怎么知道？」秦雁道：「我爹也是打猎的。我这个名字，就是他起的——他说雁是天上最难射的东西，一辈子没射着过一只。」她说着，竟笑了一笑，「他要是看见今天这一场，准说：那小子，拿一条胳膊换一只雁。」

执事唱了一声：「秦雁，负。」三年，一个字。台下有人叹了口气。人堆里一个嗓子：「你……你把秦师姐打下去了？」是孙二狗。他脸色发白，「那半块干粮……我还没还她。」小满站在台边，左臂上的血顺着指尖往下滴，一句话也答不上来。秘境里伸进坑里拉他上来的，就是方才递回去的那一截剑鞘。

她转身要走，又停住了，背对着他，声音压得低低的：「四强，你跟马小宝一个半边。你怀里揣着的，不管是什么，捂紧了。」

老槐树底下，钱掌柜拿炭条把木板上的名字划得只剩几行：**祁长松　一赔一。马小宝　一赔四。**内门那个七层，一赔三。沈小满那一行，他把「二十」抹了，写上一个「五」。有人挤上来嚷：「掌柜的，我晌午押的是二十！」钱掌柜眼皮也不抬：「押出去的，照押出去的算。」
story.en:
This bout was nothing like the last. Qin Yan's sword was a real sword, her moves real moves — a low-tier magic weapon, and in her hand, when the point went out, the green breath on the blade ran three feet further; a man a full pace away had its edge at his face already. Thrust after thrust, fast and steady, till the crowd held its breath. Xiaoman didn't watch her sword; he watched her feet: wherever the sword was going, the foot moved first; wherever the foot moved, the shoulder dipped first. But her feet were far cleaner than Lu Fang's, small quick shifts; he could see them, and his body was always half a step behind. At the seventh move the point slit his sleeve; at the fifteenth, his shoulder; at the twentieth a cut opened across his right cheek, warm, and ran into his collar. A sign held in each hand, he couldn't parry, only dodge: a hop here, a roll there — he dodged very badly, twice practically scrambling on all fours.

At the twenty-second move Qin Yan's left hand twisted, and three ice spikes shot at him together. Xiaoman slapped a palm on the bluestone and a stretch of earth wall heaved up before him; the spikes went into it — thup, thup, thup; his other hand had already sprouted a ball of fire, thrown at her feet — and in the instant she jumped clear he won back half a step. Someone below yelled: "Two kinds! Two kinds again!" Qin Yan landed and gave him one look, and in that look was surprise.

One thrust came too fast to read her feet; he could only fling himself back, and the point went past the tip of his nose and sheared off a lock of hair from his forehead. The lock floated down and down, off the stage, and landed right on A He's notebook. She glanced at it and, deadpan, tucked it between the pages. On the hand that held her pencil, the thumbnail had been dug all along into the palm of the other hand.

But dodging and dodging, Xiaoman felt something he had never had since he could remember: he was smiling. Again and again the point went past under his nose, beside his ears; he was cut all over, the rib hurt at every breath, and still the corners of his mouth turned up — for the first time, across from him stood someone stronger, and every move was real, nothing hidden, nothing given, wanting nothing from him. He turned with that sword like following his father through the woods after the finest deer, and the chase set his chest burning. Below, they held their breath at first; then someone shouted "Good!", and then whole stretches of them were shouting.

At the thirtieth move he was driven to the edge at last. Under his heels, half an inch of bluestone; behind that, frozen earth. Qin Yan's point rested on his throat, cold. The crowd went silent.

In her right sleeve, all along, Qin Yan had held a yellow paper thunder talisman, a thin blue light swimming in its cinnabar lines, from the first move to this one, and never drawn it. Xiaoman was one sword's length from her; he could see its corner peeping from her cuff. She glanced down below the stage: in the front row crouched a few children just come through the gate, mouths open, staring up at her, packed under the rim of the stage, less than an arm from the bluestone. The talisman she didn't draw. Xiaoman's right hand hung in his sleeve; his fingers touched the three tickle needles, rested there a moment, and let go.

She didn't need to. With the point on his throat she had only to push one inch, and he could only step back; one step back, and he was off. That inch was the very thing on A He's page: two contests, four bouts won, every one the same. He had known since the stove mouth that morning that this inch was coming; what to pay for it, he had decided himself.

Xiaoman didn't step back. In the instant the point came forward, he went to meet it — not with his throat; he turned his body and took it on his left arm. The point went into the outside of his left arm and came out the other side, and the pain whited out his sight. But he was already in front of Qin Yan, and with the left hand the sword ran through, he seized the scabbard in her left hand.

Qin Yan started and pulled — the blade was stuck in his arm and wouldn't come; she let the sword go and chopped at his wrist, and he didn't let go; and there at the edge the two of them grappled, no moves at all, just hands, elbows, shoulders, knees, like two children fighting over a rabbit in the mud. Her elbow struck his chest and hit something hard — and hot. Qin Yan was taller and steadier, and in three or four heaves had him half hanging off the stage. Xiaoman hooked a foot — the hook a hunter uses on a snared rabbit's leg — around her ankle. They both tipped outward together.

Xiaoman's left hand held the scabbard; his right caught the stone rim. Qin Yan's toe touched the edge once and found no hold.

She landed on the frozen earth below — landed on her feet, without a single stagger. Xiaoman hung from the rim, half his body over, her sword still through his left arm. The incense had only a dot of red left.

The steward swallowed, and struck the gong: "…Qin Yan leaves the stage. Shen Xiaoman wins."

Below, a moment's silence, and then a roar louder than the one for Lu Fang, wave on wave, rolling from one end of the training ground to the other.

Below the stage Qin Yan looked down at her hand, then up at Xiaoman, a long while. Xiaoman climbed back up, drew the sword out of his arm, turned it and held out the hilt to her, the scabbard with it, and said low: "Sister." Qin Yan took the sword. "Off the stage, you lose. By the rules, I've lost." She glanced at the hand hanging at his side and said quietly: "Nobody at layer four lasts thirty moves against me. Those eyes of yours weren't trained on a practice ground." "You too, sister." He glanced at her cuff. Her eyebrow lifted slightly; with her left hand she pressed the cuff down and let that pass. "Those steps of yours — hunter's steps, aren't they?" Xiaoman started. "How do you know, sister?" "My father hunts too. He gave me my name — he said the wild goose is the hardest thing in the sky to shoot; he never hit one in his life." And she actually smiled. "If he'd seen this bout today, he'd say: that boy traded an arm for a goose."

The steward called out: "Qin Yan — lost." Three years: one word. Someone below sighed. From the crowd a voice: "You… you knocked Sister Qin down?" It was Sun Ergou, white in the face. "That half ration… I never paid her back." Xiaoman stood at the edge, the blood from his left arm dripping off his fingertips, and couldn't answer a word. The scabbard that had reached down into the pit in the hidden realm and pulled him out was the one he had just handed back.

She turned to go, then stopped with her back to him and spoke low: "In the last four, you and Ma Xiaobao are in the same half. Whatever you've got in your coat, hold it tight."

Under the pagoda tree Money-Keeper Qian struck names off the board in charcoal till only a few lines were left: **Qi Changsong, one to one. Ma Xiaobao, one to four.** The inner-court layer seven, one to three. On Shen Xiaoman's line he rubbed out "twenty" and wrote "five." Someone pushed up shouting: "Keeper, I put mine down at twenty at noon!" Without lifting his eyelids: "What went out at a price is reckoned at that price."
